content: Cellulitis and erysipelas are now generally regarded as different manifestations of the same condition, which is a bacterial skin infection characterized by significant pain and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Various antibiotic regimens are recommended in clinical guidelines for the treatment of these infections. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatments for cellulitis that is not acquired through surgical procedures. A systematic search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted in May 2010 using databases such as the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and ongoing trial registries. The inclusion criteria for the review were RCTs that compared two or more different treatment interventions for cellulitis. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data. A total of 25 studies involving 2,488 participants were included in the analysis. The primary outcome, which was the resolution of symptoms as rated by either the participant or a medical practitioner, or the proportion of participants who became symptom-free, was commonly reported across the studies. However, no two trials evaluated the exact same drugs, so the analysis grouped similar classes of antibiotics together. Macrolides and streptogramins were found to be more effective than penicillin-based antibiotics, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.84 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73 to 0.97). In three trials involving 419 participants, two of these studies compared oral macrolides to intravenous (IV) penicillin, demonstrating that oral therapies can be more effective than IV therapies, with an RR of 0.85 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.98). Three studies, including a total of 88 participants, compared penicillin with cephalosporins and found no significant difference in treatment efficacy (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.43). Similarly, six trials involving 538 participants compared different generations of cephalosporins and found no significant differences in treatment outcomes (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.06). There were only small, single studies available for other treatment comparisons, such as the duration of antibiotic therapy, intramuscular versus intravenous administration, the addition of corticosteroids to antibiotics versus antibiotics alone, and the use of vibration therapy. Due to the limited data, no definitive conclusions could be drawn from these studies. Only two studies specifically investigated treatments for severe cellulitis, and these studies used different antibiotics for their comparisons. As a result, no firm conclusions could be made regarding the optimal treatment for severe cases. In conclusion, the review was unable to determine the best treatment for cellulitis due to the variability in study designs and the limited number of trials for certain interventions. Most treatment recommendations are based on single studies. There is a need for further trials to evaluate the effectiveness of oral antibiotics compared to intravenous antibiotics in community settings, as this has implications for both healthcare costs and patient comfort.
